questions.prompt: Closed-loop bandwidth \(\omega_b\) is the frequency where
options: \(|T(j\omega)|\) has fallen to \(1/\sqrt{2}\) of its low-frequency value
questions.explanation: Bandwidth is a property of the complementary sensitivity \(T\), 3 dB below the low-frequency plateau. The frequency where \(|L| = 1\) is the gain crossover, which is related but not the same definition. Phase of \(-180^\circ\) is the phase crossover. The peak of \(|S|\) is the peak sensitivity, not the bandwidth.

questions.prompt: At the gain crossover, \(|S| = 1/(2\sin(\mathrm{PM}/2))\). For a phase margin of \(36^\circ\) that sensitivity is
questions.explanation: Half of \(36^\circ\) is \(18^\circ\), and \(\sin 18^\circ \approx 0.309\), so \(|S| = 1/(2\cdot 0.309) = 1.61803\). Using \(\sin 36^\circ\) in the denominator forgets the half-angle in the distance formula. The phase margin itself, 36, is a number of degrees, not a sensitivity.

questions.prompt: A first-order closed loop has bandwidth 5 rad/s. Its 10% to 90% rise time is about \(2.2/\omega_b\), which equals
questions.explanation: \(t_r \approx 2.2/5 = 0.44\) s. The reciprocal of the bandwidth, 0.2 s, is the time constant, and the 10% to 90% rise is \(\ln 9\) time constants, not one. Twice the bandwidth in the denominator would give 0.22 s and is a different rule of thumb.

questions.prompt: The loop transfer function is \(L(s) = 12/s\). The gain crossover frequency, where \(|L| = 1\), is
questions.explanation: \(|L(j\omega)| = 12/\omega\). Setting that equal to 1 gives \(\omega_c = 12\) rad/s. The square root of 12 is a different crossover, for a \(1/s^2\) loop. Half of 12 would be the crossover of \(6/s\).

questions.prompt: A specification \(M_s \le 1.5\) limits how close the Nyquist curve may come to \(-1\). A larger allowed \(M_s\) means
options: the curve must stay farther from \(-1\)
the curve may come closer to \(-1\), so the robustness demand is weaker
the bandwidth must be cut in half
the phase margin must be exactly 90 degrees
questions.explanation: Peak sensitivity is the reciprocal of the distance from the curve to \(-1\). Allowing a larger peak allows a smaller distance. The stricter spec is the smaller \(M_s\). Bandwidth is not fixed by \(M_s\) alone, and a 90 degree phase margin is a much stronger requirement than \(M_s = 1.5\).

questions.prompt: The design requires \(M_s \le 1.5\). The Nyquist curve must therefore stay at least this far from \(-1\):
questions.explanation: The distance is \(1/M_s = 1/1.5 = 0.666667\). The peak 1.5 itself is the reciprocal of the distance, not the distance. Twice the reciprocal, \(1.333\), doubles the clearance the spec actually demands.

questions.prompt: Tracking and disturbance rejection both want \(|L|\) large at low frequency. Sensor-noise rejection wants
options: \(|L|\) large at high frequency as well
\(|T|\) small at high frequency, which means \(|L|\) small there
the crossover as high as the actuator can stand, with no further condition
questions.explanation: Noise enters through \(T\). Making \(|T|\) small at high frequency means rolling \(|L|\) off. Keeping \(|L|\) large up there would pass the noise. A large \(|S|\) is the high-frequency fate of every proper loop, not a design goal by itself. Crossover has to stop somewhere because of that noise, the actuator, and the phase lag.

questions.prompt: At a frequency where the loop gain is real and equal to 0.25, the complementary sensitivity \(|T|\) is
questions.explanation: \(T = L/(1+L) = 0.25/1.25 = 0.2\). The sensitivity \(S = 1/1.25 = 0.8\) is the other closed-loop map. The loop gain 0.25 itself is not \(T\).

questions.prompt: The gain crossover has a phase margin of \(50^\circ\). The phase of \(L\) at that frequency, in degrees, is
questions.explanation: Phase margin is the distance above \(-180^\circ\), so the phase is \(-180 + 50 = -130\). Reporting \(+50\) gives the margin rather than the phase. Reporting \(-50\) measures down from 0 instead of up from \(-180\).

questions.prompt: The crossover formula \(|S| = 1/(2\sin(\mathrm{PM}/2))\) is required to be at most 1.4. The smallest phase margin that meets the formula, in degrees, is
questions.explanation: Set \(1/(2\sin(\mathrm{PM}/2)) = 1.4\), so \(\sin(\mathrm{PM}/2) = 1/2.8\). Then \(\mathrm{PM}/2 \approx 20.92^\circ\) and \(\mathrm{PM} = 41.8497\). Using the half-angle as the answer reports about 20.9 degrees. A margin of 60 degrees gives \(|S| = 1\), which is stricter than 1.4.

questions.prompt: Raising the gain crossover, while the plant phase is still falling, usually
options: leaves both bandwidth and overshoot unchanged
removes the need for a roll-off at high frequency
speeds the response and spends phase margin
questions.explanation: A higher crossover uses a frequency where a typical plant has more lag, so the phase margin shrinks, while the closed-loop bandwidth and the speed both go up. The margin does not increase. Overshoot tends to grow as the margin shrinks. The high-frequency roll-off is still required, and it gets harder as the crossover moves up.

questions.prompt: Below 2 rad/s the spec is \(|S| \le 0.1\), and \(L\) is real and positive. The smallest such \(L\) that makes \(|S| = 0.1\) is
questions.explanation: \(1/(1+L) = 0.1\) gives \(1+L = 10\) and \(L = 9\). The value 10 is \(1+L\), one step short of the loop gain. The value 0.1 is the sensitivity spec itself.
